In the queue outside the chemistry lab, Vaibhav leaned over and grinned. "So, Yamini, is it true your dad moved out and your mum works nights now? Charu said you cry about it in the washroom."
Yamini's stomach dropped like a lift. For a second the corridor went quiet in her ears. She had told exactly one person that, in a whisper, sitting on the terrace steps in August.
She looked down the line. Charu was laughing with the new girls at the front, ponytail swinging, the same Charu who had cried with her that day. Now she looked like someone Yamini had never met.
"Who told you?" Yamini asked, though she knew.
Vaibhav shrugged. "Everyone knows."
When Ms Reddy opened the lab door, Yamini walked in, sat at the back bench and stared at the burner for the whole period, face hot, eyes stinging.

I'm Nathan, Elizabeth's older brother, and I've never seen her the way she was on Tuesday. She came home, dropped her bag in the hallway and went straight to her laptop. When I looked over her shoulder, she was typing a post about Anjali, something about Anjali's mum and the shop. Her jaw was tight and her hands were quick.

I'm Yamini, and my little brother Vaibhav is fifteen. On Thursday his best friend Dhruv came to our door, which he never does without messaging first. I was in the kitchen and heard most of it.
Dhruv said quietly, "You told Neel about my speech classes."
Vaibhav's first answer was, "Bro, relax, it was a joke, you're making it a whole thing." Dhruv didn't say anything. He just started putting his shoes back on.
Then Vaibhav said, "Wait." There was a long pause. I think he was trying to find the words. "I did tell Neel. It was wrong. I wanted everyone to laugh. I'm really ashamed."
Dhruv stopped with one shoe on. I couldn't see his face. After a minute he said, "Okay," and they sat on the steps for a while without talking.
I don't know what either of them felt. I just know that "wait" changed something.

The staffroom at St. Anne's emptied fast after the last bell. Devika packed her marking into her bag while Wasim hovered by the kettle.
"Coffee on Saturday? Like old times?" he asked.
It had been eight months since he told the principal about her private complaint. He'd apologised, a quick "sorry if you were hurt", and then, three weeks ago, she'd heard he had passed on something about Mrs Joseph too.
Devika zipped the bag. "I don't think so, Wasim. I'm glad for the years we had. But I'm not going to keep being close."
He looked stung. "Because of one thing?"
"Because it wasn't one thing." She said it gently. She wasn't angry any more; she'd done that part in the winter.
On the way out she stopped at the library to return a book to Ms Pinto, who had become the person she called on hard days. It felt like choosing well.
